learningObjective: Distinguish latency from throughput and identify architectural strategies that optimize one at the expense of the other.

canonicalClaims.claim: Latency is per-item completion time; throughput is completed-items-per-unit-time. Pipelining and parallelism can raise throughput without lowering latency, and critical path (sequential dependencies) sets a latency floor.
conditions: The workload has both a critical path and parallelizable structure.
Comparison is meaningful only when specifying which axis (latency or throughput) is being optimized.
nonImplications: Does not imply reciprocal relation between latency and throughput.
Does not imply CPUs always beat GPUs on latency for every task.

misconceptions.whyWrong: In a pipelined system with N stages, throughput can be N/latency; parallelism further decouples the two.
Sequential dependencies (critical path) bound latency regardless of worker count; parallelism helps throughput on independent items.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Amdahl's Law analogue on latency vs throughput

misconceptions.claim: GPUs have lower per-op latency than CPUs for any workload.
misconceptions.whyWrong: GPUs optimize aggregate throughput; single-op latency (with kernel launch and pipeline depth) can be worse than an in-order CPU running a scalar op.

implementationFacts: Little's Law: N = X · L (concurrency = throughput · latency).
Pipelined systems: steady-state throughput ≈ 1 / (slowest stage) once filled.
performanceScenarios: LLM prefill has high throughput (batched compute) but not necessarily lower TTFT; TPOT and throughput trade off against each other.
